newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-ANDERSEN MATCHPLAY GOLF GOES ACCORDING TO SEEDING.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ANDERSEN MATCHPLAY GOLF GOES ACCORDING TO SEEDING.

text.p: All four matches at the international regional of the Andersen Consulting World Championship of Golf Monday went according to the seedings but not one of them was decided until the 18th hole.

Australians Greg Norman and Steve Elkington, U.S. Open champion Ernie Els of South Africa and Nick Price of Zimbabwe -- all ranked among the top seven players in the world -- advanced to the international semifinals with victories on the River Course at Blackwolf Run.
None of them, however, had an easy time.
"I knew we were going to get to number 18," Price said. "It was a question of who would make a mistake."
He could have been speaking for everyone.
Price beat Vijay Singh of Fiji, 1-up, when Singh bogeyed the 469-yard, par-four 18th hole.
Els beat Frank Nobilo of New Zealand, 1-up, when Nobilo bogeyed the final hole.
The match between Elkington and Mark McNulty of Zimbabwe ended the same way: McNulty made a bogey and Elkington won, 1-up.
Norman led 1-up going into the 18th against fellow Australian Robert Allenby. Norman made a par, Allenby made a bogey, and Norman won 2-up.
"The round," Norman said, "could have gone either way."

The semifinalists meet Tuesday morning on the River Course. Top seed Norman, ranked second in the world, faces seventh-ranked, fourth seed Elkington. Els, ranked third and seeded second, faces fifth-ranked, third seed Price.

The championship match is set for later Tuesday, with the winner earning $200,000 and advancing to the Andersen world finals, January 3-4, 1998, in Scottsdale, Arizona. The overall champion collects a total of $1 million.
Colin Montgomerie (Europe), Davis Love (United States) and Hajime Meshiai (Japan) already have won their respective regionals.
The 6,991-yard, par-72 River Course, designed by Pete Dye and opened in 1988, proved to be an interesting venue for match play.
With a mix of relatively easy holes and difficult ones -- the latter compounded by a tricky wind and severely sloping greens -- there was plenty of variance in the scores.
The four matches produced three eagles, 26 birdies, 20 bogeys, three double-bogeys and 1 triple-bogey.
"The margin for error here is marginal," Els said. "It's a course where if you go at it and pull it off, you'll probably have a good chance for birdie. But if you don't, you'll be in trouble.
"If you miss a shot by a couple of yards, you're bound to make bogey, or worse."
Despite the rollercoaster rides, no golfer ever had more than a two-hole lead.
